newsitem.title: USA: Twin threats, canker and Medflies, plague Florida.
newsitem.headline: Twin threats, canker and Medflies, plague Florida.

text.p: Florida's $6 billion agriculture industry was under a double threat Wednesday as a Mediterranean fruit fly infestation expanded and an outbreak of citrus canker was confirmed, officials said.
The twin menaces were confined to a small region around Tampa on the state's west coast, but the Medfly threatened to move into Florida's citrus-growing heartland.

Agriculture officials said the war against the Medfly, launched with an aerial spraying program last week, had not gone as planned and the infestation had spread from largely urban areas near Tampa east to the Polk County line. Polk County is Florida's top producer of citrus.
Richard Clark, director of the state's Medfly program, said a runaway infestation could destroy Florida's citrus export trade.
"If we don't clear this up quickly, many of our export markets will be eliminated," Clark said. "They're watching us, watching what we do, I guarantee you."

Officials also confirmed an outbreak of citrus canker in three groves in Manatee County, between Tampa and Sarasota, and said it might be a recurrence of a 1991 outbreak that led to the burning of entire citrus groves.

The first aerial spraying of large areas of Tampa and nearby suburbs with the pesticide malathion had killed 90 percent of adult Medflies in the area, Richard Clark, director of the state's Medfly program, said.

But new flies continued to appear outside the treatment zone, forcing officials to expand the area being sprayed. Initially about 50 square miles, the spray zone had been extended to 120 square miles.
Officials said the eradication program, expected to last 60 days and cost $4 million, was extended to six months and would cost $6 million.
"This is no time to cut corners," Richard Gaskalla, director of the Department of Agriculture's Division of Plant Industries, said.

The Medfly, harmless to humans, is considered one of the most economically damaging pests because it tolerates cold weather and feeds on some 250 types of fruit and vegetables, including citrus and tomatoes, Florida's largest cash crops.
Three helicopters, equipped with global positioning devices to guide their flight, will repeatedly spray a malathion bait on the affected area for the next 60 days.
On the ground, an army of state agriculture employees, migrant workers and jail prisoners were stripping fruit off trees where Medfly larvae have been found.
The citrus canker outbreak appeared to be the Asian or "A" strain of the bacterial disease, which kills trees and discolors fruit, making it unmarketable, officials said.
"I would guess it is a reoccurrence of the outbreak we had in 1991," Gaskalla said.
The only way to get rid of the disease is to burn the trees, officials said. In 1991, entire groves were torched to contain the most recent commercially damaging outbreak.
A stubborn canker outbreak has been fought in residential areas of central Dade County for the last two years. Hundreds of backyard trees have been cut down and burned.
